item.content:encoded:
This week, Brisbane’s indie-folk vocalist Lottie McLeod dropped her second EP The Boathouse, a body of work that sees the artist honing in on her delicate sound. Right before the EP dropped, we sat down with Lottie to discuss the tender collection of tracks chronicling love-bombing, yearning and the irresistible draw of Manly Boathouse.
Tell us about the story behind the album name and the artwork for The Boathouse EP.
It’s called The Boathouse because I subconsciously always bring people to the Manly Boathouse when I want to have a discussion that’s not lighthearted. I always, for some reason, gravitate to that area.
The first lyric of the song ‘Boathouse’ is, we get along and we talk it out by the boathouse. That lyric was written before I decided the title, so I thought that would all tie it together.
The cover art was really unintentional. I knew that I wanted it to be in a watery sort of area, and it wasn’t until a couple of weeks later I realised that I took it at Wynnum, right next to the boathouse. I was like, oh, I should just run with that and tell people I did it on purpose, but it was accidental.
What is it about Manly Boathouse you find yourself going back to?
My first boyfriend lived five minutes away, so we went there a couple of times, and then for some reason, everyone who has had some sort of important role in my life has always lived near that area too. So it’s just been somewhere we can meet in the middle and it’s just really grounding. I’m a water baby, I always have been, so anywhere near the water will always be really grounding to me and bring some sort of ease and calmness.
Can you tell us the best lesson you learnt while putting together the EP?
In this EP you’ll hear that I’m a very trusting person, maybe a little bit too much sometimes. I let people in and I take their word for all the good things they’re saying, which isn’t a bad quality to have but I definitely learnt to put myself first and learnt from a lot of experiences like love bombing, for example.
A lot of these songs came from love bombing and I know that’s such a modern word, but it’s so common. It happens to everyone and it’s not a lighthearted thing. So I learnt to think more about who I let into my life, not in a toxic way but in a way where I’m choosing myself first.
The Boathouse will be your second EP in as many years; how has your sound and style changed over that time?
When I recorded Bug, I was very new to being in the studio, and I still am now but I was a baby who had never done anything like that before. Sometimes I was scared to use my voice, and I also hadn’t really made any close enough connections with producers that I could just throw a really whack idea out there.
With this EP, I’ve learned that I don’t need to have lots of major intense theory knowledge and be the most knowledgeable in the room. I can just say what I’m thinking and if a sound comes into my head that I think sounds cool I can just say it. I’ve developed a team of people that I can say anything to, like my producer Josh Beattie – he will never look at me like I’m a weirdo and we’ve really built a sound that sounds more like me.
Where was the EP recorded?
It’s a seven track EP and five of the songs were recorded at 4000 Studios, so a big chunk of it was there with Josh Beattie. The other two songs were recorded in North Carolina, actually, with Caleb Wright at a really, really beautiful studio in Durham.
The music video for ‘Wednesdays at the Waterloo’ looks like it was a fun one to film. Can you tell me what your favourite part of that process was?
Well, all of the extras are just really close friends of mine, so it honestly just felt like a really cool hang. To be honest, I didn’t see what they were doing in the video because I was looking at the camera, but when I watched it back, they just got into it so much. They’re all incredible actors, and they just made the music video what it was.
I’ve never really had any ideas of what I want my music videos to look like. Most of my music videos before ‘Wednesdays’, I haven’t been too proud of and acting in front of the camera is something that I haven’t ever been too comfortable doing. But with ‘Wednesdays’ I was able to incorporate my own idea and also feel a lot more confident in front of the camera, and I can watch it and not cringe, which is really good.
Subscribe for updates
You’ve got a big couple of months coming up with the release of your EP. How do you manage such a busy schedule, and does it help or hinder your creative process?
Yeah, it’s very, very hectic. I’m very lucky that I have just the best team. It’s a small team but they’re all so willing to take a load off my plate when I need to.
I’m not going to lie, sometimes it does have an effect on my creative process. Sometimes when I’m so focused on the songs I’m promoting, I can feel a little bit burnt out. I also work almost 30 hours a week, so it can get very tricky, but last night I wrote a song that I’m really, really proud of, and there’s little moments like that where I’m like, oh, I’ve still got it, I haven’t lost my push and drive for it.
I love writing, and I think it’s really important. I always take at least half an hour a day to sit and play, and even if it’s just playing a cover of a song that I really love.
What would you say is your favourite venue in Brisbane to play?
There’s so many. Maybe this is a hot take, but I love playing at Black Bear Lodge. I started there, and for a while there, I was playing it all the time, and I kind of got over it. Then I didn’t play there for probably a good year, and I played there a few weeks ago, and it was really nice. Everyone starts their Brisbane live music experience there and it feels really sentimental.
Now, if you could only pick three songs to take with you on a deserted island, what would you pick?
The first one is ‘The King of Wishful Thinking’ by Go West. That’s one of my favourite songs of all time, it always feels like the first time listening to it.
Can I swear? There’s a song called ‘Coolest fucking bitch in town’ by Haley Blais. That’s a song I discovered in high school, and then it wasn’t until last year I listened to that album in full, and it’s one of my favourite albums of all time.
And I can’t not say a Samia song, she’s my favourite. I’d have to say ‘Proof’ by Samia.
If you were tasked with creating a dream team of Brisbane artists, who would you want on your team?
Meiia. It sounds biassed because she’s my best friend, but I genuinely am just obsessed with her music, I listen to her demos all the time. She’s just moved from Cairns, and she’s a crack songwriter. She’s just put out a song called ‘Fix It Anyway’, and it’s about how AI sucks, but not in a cringe way.
What are you looking forward to on The Boathouse tour?
Well, I’m playing smaller venues, and I am really excited to just see the people. I did my own tour last year, but I also supported a band called Peach Fuzz, and I feel like I got some people listening from that tour, so it’ll be really cool to see those faces again.
Honestly, touring just feels like a holiday to me. It’s just like a big holiday with my band, and also my friends, and Meiia is playing Sydney and Brisbane, so it’ll just be like a holiday with my best friends. I’m literally counting down the days.
Lottie McLeod’s The Boathouse EP officially drops on Friday September 25, with the tour kicking off in October, where she will play Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, with support from LILY B, Meiia, Franjapan, Grace de Vos and Kieran Stevenson. She will also be supporting both The Tullarmarines and Peter Garrett & The Alter Egos on their tours across November.

item.content:encoded:
Dear Abby | Teacher suspects parents’ phone habits affect kids
Today's advice from Dear Abby.
DEAR ABBY: You sometimes ask readers to share their pet peeves. I am a public school teacher, and here is mine: Parents wonder why their children misbehave, argue with them and act out with attention-getting behaviors. My advice to them: Put down those cellphones and pay attention to your kids!
I just had a conference with a mother whose children argue, pout and scream when they are told to do something at home. These children have no special needs and don’t demonstrate those behaviors at school. Abby, the woman texted on her phone throughout the meeting. That behavior is not OK.
The next time I encounter a parent who does it, I will ask the person if he or she would like to suspend the conference to take care of the pressing business. Perhaps these parents need to be embarrassed a bit so they will realize how inappropriate texting or talking on the phone is when face-to-face with another person.
— A VENTING EDUCATOR
DEAR EDUCATOR: I agree that what the parent did was extremely rude. It sent the unmistakable message that not only was the meeting not important to her, but neither was anything you had to say. If you are asking me for permission to inform parents that cellphones must be silenced and out of sight during conferences with you, you have it. My advice is to say it as soon as the parent enters your classroom. You can frame it as parents following the same rules as students in your space.
** ** **
DEAR ABBY: I have three grown children. One son, “Charles,” with his wife and three elementary-school-aged children, rents the house next door to me for about $1,200 a month less than I might charge a nonfamily renter. My other two kids live hundreds of miles away. My younger son, “James,” is unmarried and without children. He thinks I’m being unfair to him and his sister because I’m not charging the maximum rent the house might get, thereby reducing his inheritance. I place great value in having Charles and his family living next door to me. James thinks I should be regularly compensating him and his sister for what he claims I’m giving to Charles and his family. What do you think?
— LANDLORD DAD
DEAR LANDLORD DAD: I think it’s presumptuous and ill-mannered of your younger son to count his inheritance while his father is still living and breathing. Charles’ rent is between you and him, and frankly, James shouldn’t be privy to the details of the arrangement. Tell your grasping younger son that every time he brings this up in the future, you’ll deduct $1,200 from his share of the estate and divide it between Charles and his sister.
** ** **
DEAR ABBY: I have two daughters, ages 19 and 21. They both have jobs. My husband and I would like them to help pay for a family vacation because they expect expensive experiences. Are we wrong to ask them to contribute?
— HELPING OUT IN NEW YORK
DEAR HELPING: I don’t think it would be wrong to enlighten your daughters about what the family vacation is costing. If their expectations will uncomfortably strain your budget, explain that you will need them to chip in so they can experience everything they want.

item.content:encoded:
Each sign of the zodiac has its own set of traits that help to define their personalities and set them apart from each other. Wouldn't it be nice to know what the universe has planned for you at the beginning of the day? Keep reading to find out if today will be lucky for you.
ARIES
Love is real even while loving is silent. Today need steady activity, not excessive drama. If you are devoted, show you care with modest kindnesses of aid, rapid response and strong planning. If single, say yes to quiet chats or time together over coffee. Don’t get into crashes to establish who’s point is right. You are at your best when you feel called to listen and then communicate plainly. The evening’s open discussions on future hopes
TAURUS
Today is about presence, not performance. Put your phone away and listen to your sweetheart or date completely. Keep the voice cool, ask straightforward questions, and get the answers. If you’re single, pick a place where socializing isn’t hurried. No need for flash. True connection is based on continuous eye contact and a little patience. Light plans for the week. By evening the feeling flows down gently as the occasion speaks for itself.
GEMINI
An emotional truth communicated will build the intended relationship. Say it in your feeling terms .
If something is upsetting you, say something, don't blame. If you are single, you need to be fairly clear about how fast or slow you go in terms of dating and what your boundaries are. Usually it is a thrill to engage in the lighthearted company of interested discourse. Today, however, you are bound to ask one truly crucial question and answer it genuinely yourself.
CANCER
You can wish to be more than picked. Demand equal effort. If you do decide to commit, talk about time, money and plans honestly and openly. If you are single, don’t settle for confused sentiments. The nurturing is strong here, but today calls for a clean cut. You want to say what you need in love in a soft yet firm way. Time spent at home will be a comfort to you. A promise carefully maintained and on schedule will show who really values you. Your heart deserves a mate, it is no longer willing to be left in the shadows.
LEO
A little item might mean more than a lot of big talk. Talk is cheap, but today, actions are cheap too. Send a text, book a table or buy a treat. Singles, just say hi and show some real interest. Keep stories short. Smile with your eyes. Sharing attention allows the charm shine. Simple and punctual evening arrangements run nicely. Now it counts for loyalty. Your constant spark can change a heart, no need for huge drama.
VIRGO
Be open-hearted but not open-exposed. Share sentiments in stages, and with clear boundaries. If you are serious, prepare a practical week and distribute the tasks equitably. If you’re single, pick a safe place and keep the first dates brief. You don’t have to fix anyone. Polite truth is enough. Keep your messaging clean timing should be right and so should punctuation. Soft romance is conducive to the neat mind. A warm mug of tea and honest talk will dispel doubts and create trust.
LIBRA
Whatever you feel is valid. Even if it is messy. Balance is good; today, choose truth above a flawless picture. Say apologize if necessary, seek for support where you struggle if coupled. If you are single don’t keep hiding your confusion because you want to please someone. To begin the alleviation, the first step will be a short text recognizing confused sentiments. Choose a calm spot with soft music when you go for a conversation. Let the scales move on their own.
SCORPIO
If you find yourself caught up in an emotionally taxing habit, today is a wonderful day to start creating some distance. If you are committed, stop a heated discussion, and perhaps re-start it when cooler heads have prevailed. If you're single, stay away from people who keep you guessing. Your depth is precious, invest it where trust flourishes. Keep plans light and on the down low. A excellent friend might offer you a hefty dose of reality. Listen up.
SAGITTARIUS
Don’t mix chemistry with compatibility. Sparks are exhilarating, but daily living calls for corresponding values. Ask about overall time goals and family opinions on financial style if you're dating. If you are, re-ignite your common ambitions with a little bit of planning for the weekend. Travel talk is nice, but it’s important to nail down the dates before you throw in the towel on huge goals. Keep the hilarious lines going and keep a close eye out for red signals.
CAPRICORN
A touch of tenderness would very much affect the entire tone. A steady nature is recognized; thus today, add a pleasant word and a soft touch. Partnered? Check feelings, not tasks. Schedule 5 minutes. If you are single, attempt a quick note to indicate you really are interested. Work is a drain, so put a time restriction on your calls. Good sense is good, but display good sense in tiny ways. The evening will be peaceful, so it is possible to resolve conflicts and agree on the next step.
AQUARIUS
You can hold room for someone and not lose yourself. If coupled, listen completely and then communicate your boundaries plainly. If you are single, keep your discussions cordial, but don't overextend yourself beyond your energies. Set up a basic meeting that you can leave on time. Today, thoughts are coming swiftly, jot them down yet stay with the individual. Little habits like quick responses develop trust. Shower your love in plain words
PISCES
Speak your love language out loud, don’t expect others to read it. What do you do that brings you close? If you do, offer two little activities you can both accomplish every day. Single? Tell us what kind of date suits you. Don't allude. Words are important. Clear words. Music or art can pull the tone together today. Keep hopes grounded, pay attention to time when reacting. Lead the tone with straightforward clarity, and your particular someone will understand and meet you halfway.
This article is written by, Sidhharrth S Kumaar, Registered Pharmacist, Astro Numerologist, Life & Relationship Coach, Vaastu Expert, IKS Expert, I Ching Expert, Energy Healer, Music Therapist, Author of “Think like a Sage Lead like a CEO” series and Chief Astro Strategy Officer (CASO), NumroVani.

item.content:encoded:
Love may feel like it is developing gradually rather than dramatically. If you're single, give a promising connection time to reveal its potential. Couples may need patience while waiting for an emotional or practical situation to mature.
Love Horoscope Today, September 21, 2026: Love may deepen through emotional balance, trust, and understanding today
Love Horoscope Today: Daily astrological predictions for all sun signs for September 21, 2026, find what your stars says.
Love Tip: Don't abandon something meaningful simply because it needs time.
Crystal Remedy: Moss Agate: Keep it nearby to encourage patience and steady emotional growth.
The past may return through a memory, message, or familiar person. This could bring warmth and comfort, but it may also make you question what you still feel. Let nostalgia inform your understanding without allowing it to make your romantic decisions for you.
Love Tip: Appreciate the past without living inside it.
Crystal Remedy: Rhodonite: Carry it to encourage emotional balance and compassionate reflection.
A relationship chapter may be reaching an important milestone or conclusion. Singles could feel ready to move beyond an old pattern, while couples may experience a renewed sense of completion after resolving something that has lingered.
Love Tip: Allow closure to create room for something healthier.
Crystal Remedy: Labradorite: Keep it close when beginning a new romantic chapter to symbolize transition and a fresh perspective.
You may be drawn toward relationships that offer genuine stability and care. Singles could notice someone dependable, while couples may focus on home, finances, or practical plans for the future.
Love Tip: Value consistency as much as chemistry.
Crystal Remedy: Green Jade: Keep it in your bedroom to encourage harmony, stability, and nurturing affection.
A new romantic possibility could appear in an unexpected form. Singles may receive an interesting message or invitation, while couples can refresh their connection by learning or trying something new together.
Love Tip: Stay curious about where a small beginning could lead.
Crystal Remedy: Golden Calcite: Carry it when meeting someone new to encourage optimism and openness.
You may be emotionally ready to move away from a draining romantic pattern. Singles could feel more peaceful after releasing an old attachment, while couples may need to leave past arguments behind and focus on rebuilding calm.
Love Tip: Choose the connection that brings you peace, not confusion.
Crystal Remedy: Aquamarine: Keep it close during emotional transitions to encourage calm and clarity.
Independence becomes attractive today. You may feel more confident in your own company, which can actually strengthen your romantic choices. Singles should avoid settling simply because they dislike being alone.
Love Tip: A healthy relationship should complement your independence, not replace it.
Crystal Remedy: Peridot: Carry it as a reminder of self-worth, renewal, and confidence.
Reciprocity is the central theme. You may be evaluating whether affection, attention, and effort are flowing equally between you and another person. Couples can strengthen their bond by addressing imbalances honestly.
Love Tip: Give generously, but don't ignore what you need in return.
Crystal Remedy: Green Aventurine: Keep it nearby to encourage openness, balance, and mutual support.
Your confidence and magnetism are heightened. If you're single, this can be a good day to express interest rather than waiting for someone else to make the first move. Couples may rediscover excitement by taking initiative together.
Love Tip: Use your confidence to create connection, not pressure.
Crystal Remedy: Carnelian: Carry it to encourage courage, warmth, and romantic initiative.
Romantic developments may happen quickly. A message, invitation, or sudden change in circumstances could accelerate a connection. Be responsive, but don't let speed make you overlook important details.
Love Tip: Enjoy the momentum while staying emotionally grounded.
Crystal Remedy: Sunstone: Keep it with you during social or romantic outings to encourage confidence and enthusiasm.
A past relationship pattern may come back into focus, giving you a chance to understand it differently. You could feel ready to make a meaningful emotional decision or release something you've been carrying for too long.
Love Tip: Let your past teach you without allowing it to control your next choice.
Crystal Remedy: Selenite: Place it beside your bed as a symbolic reminder of clarity and emotional renewal.
You may feel overwhelmed by too many romantic possibilities, expectations, or emotional responsibilities. Singles should avoid entertaining every option simply because it is available. Couples may need to divide emotional responsibilities more fairly.
Love Tip: Choose depth over having too many possibilities at once.
Crystal Remedy: Lepidolite: Keep it near your bedside to encourage calm and emotional balance when love feels overwhelming.
Kishori Sud
(Certified Tarot Card Reader & Crystal Healer, Founder at EnigmaTarotTribe ™)
- Kishori Sud is a spiritual practitioner, intuitive guide, and journalist with over five years of experience in tarot reading and holistic healing. Sagittarius Love Horoscope Today

Recent efforts by Aries, Cancer, and Libra to improve communication are showing results, paving the way for emotional openness and romantic satisfaction. item.title: [TODAY.com] Gwyneth Paltrow Reveals Story Behind Her ‘Conscious Uncoupling’ With Chris Martin
item.dc:creator: Kimmy Yam
item.description: When Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin used the term “conscious uncoupling” to describe their separation in 2014, the phrase ended up going viral at the time, taking the internet by storm. And now, we finally have its backstory. Paltrow, 53, opened up about the term during a recent episode of podcast “Friends Keep Secrets.” It turns out, her introduction to the phrase came from a therapist that she and Martin had at the time. “Chris and I had this therapist that was really brilliant, and he sort
item.content:encoded:
When Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin used the term “conscious uncoupling” to describe their separation in 2014, the phrase ended up going viral at the time, taking the internet by storm.
And now, we finally have its backstory.
Paltrow, 53, opened up about the term during a recent episode of podcast “Friends Keep Secrets.” It turns out, her introduction to the phrase came from a therapist that she and Martin had at the time.
“Chris and I had this therapist that was really brilliant, and he sort of introduced us to the concept,” Paltrow told hosts Benny Blanco, Lil Dicky and his wife Kristin Batalucco during the Sept. 8 episode. “We just made a commitment to really put the kids first, and so what that meant was to stay a family, even though we weren’t a couple.”
Paltrow — who is currently married to writer and director Brad Falchuk, 55 — shares two children with Martin, 49. The two announced the news of the divorce through a statement on her Goop website.
“We are parents first and foremost, to two incredibly wonderful children and we ask for their and our space and privacy to be respected at this difficult time,” Paltrow and Martin wrote in the statement. “We have always conducted our relationship privately, and we hope that as we consciously uncouple and coparent, we will be able to continue in the same manner.”
Paltrow told the podcast that when she and Martin decided to get divorced, she turned to friends who came from divorced households for guidance.
“I said, ‘Tell me, what was the worst thing? What do you feel you have scars from to this day?’” Paltrow recounted. “They said the worst part was ... ‘My dad used to drop me off at the end of the driveway.’ ‘It was so tense at my birthday parties.’ ‘They never ate dinner in the same room until my college graduation, and it caused me so much pain.’”
She added that she and Martin sought to “circumvent all of that awful stuff.” Paltrow also shared one particular trying moment during the divorce in which she had to put the conscious uncoupling philosophy to work. She explained that when the family moved to Los Angeles early on in the separation, they continued to have brunch together every Sunday. One particular brunch date proved difficult.
“Chris and I were upset with each other about something – I can’t even remember what it is — and I was like, ‘This might go really off the rails,’” she recalled. “It was getting tense, and we looked at each other. We went outside on the front porch, and we’re like, ‘Let’s just not.’”
She said that the two ended up embracing.
“We just hugged,” she said. “We like fist-bumped and then we went to brunch.”
Paltrow, to be clear, did not invent the term “conscious uncoupling.” The tactic, believed to be coined by late marriage and family therapist Katherine Woodward Thomas, has long existed with therapists and counselors encouraging the mindset as part of the final stage of marriage counseling after a decision to divorce is made.
Life coach Jeanne Byrd Romero previously told TODAY.com that conscious uncoupling is a method that can help the parties heal.
“It’s really a way of moving out of blame and shame so people can transform the experience into healing and peace,” Romero said. “It can be done with just one of the partners are the couple.”

item.title: [instinctmagazine.com] Seattle’s Polyamory Proposal Could Expand Civil Rights Protections | Instinct Magazine
item.dc:creator: Eugene
item.description: Seattle is putting polyamory in the spotlight after moving a step closer to protecting people in consensual relationships involving multiple partners from discrimination. RELATED: Chris Gallant’s Past Isn’t a Problem. The Kink Shaming Is. The Seattle City Council’s Housing, Arts and Civil Rights Committee unanimously voted to send a proposal to the full council that would expand the city’s civil rights code. Among other changes, the proposal would recognize “consensual relationships with multipl
item.content:encoded:
Seattle is putting polyamory in the spotlight after moving a step closer to protecting people in consensual relationships involving multiple partners from discrimination.
RELATED: Chris Gallant’s Past Isn’t a Problem. The Kink Shaming Is.
The Seattle City Council’s Housing, Arts and Civil Rights Committee unanimously voted to send a proposal to the full council that would expand the city’s civil rights code. Among other changes, the proposal would recognize “consensual relationships with multiple partners as an element of attitudes, preferences, and practices pertaining to sexual orientation.”
That may sound straightforward, but it also raises a question that tends to cause plenty of confusion: what exactly is the difference between polyamory and polygamy?
The terms are often used interchangeably, even though they describe different concepts. Seattle’s proposal is specifically concerned with consensual relationships involving multiple partners, rather than creating a system of multiple marriages.
RELATED: James Talarico’s Trans Sports Shift: What Changed?
What does polyamory mean here?
In the context of Seattle’s proposal, polyamory refers to consensual relationships involving multiple partners.
The emphasis is on consent. The proposal specifically refers to “consensual relationships with multiple partners,” meaning the relationships covered are ones in which the people involved are aware of and agree to the arrangement.
That distinction is important because the legislation is about protecting people from discrimination based on their family and relationship structure.
Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, the bill’s sponsor, said the ordinance aims to “prohibit discrimination based on family and relationship structure as fully as possible.”
“We all know that every family is different, and we need to be clear that every family receives equal protection under the law,” Rinck said. “And chosen family is family.”
“This update reflects how people actually live,” Rinck added.
So where does polygamy fit in?
Polygamy and polyamory aren’t simply two words for exactly the same thing.
Polygamy is generally associated with marriage involving multiple spouses, while the Seattle proposal is addressing consensual relationships involving multiple partners and discrimination based on relationship or family structure.
That means the Seattle measure should not be described as an attempt to legalize multiple-spouse marriage. Instead, the proposal would add protections for people whose relationships and families fall outside more traditional structures.
And that distinction matters when discussing the legislation, because the issue before Seattle’s council is civil rights protection, not a change to the city’s marriage system.
Why are these protections being proposed?
The proposed protections would apply to areas including employment, housing, business licensure, places of public accommodation, park usage and “bias-free policing.” Under the proposal, people who experience unfair treatment could file complaints and seek a remedy through Seattle’s Office for Civil Rights.
Tyson Holman, co-chair of the Seattle Coalition for Family & Relationship Equity, testified in support of the proposal. Holman told council members that “being out” as poly can expose partners to discrimination, causing some people to “pretend to not love.”
“That’s why these protections are so important,” Holman said. “We don’t have to worry about losing our homes or our jobs or our families.”
Seattle’s Human Rights Commission had previously urged the mayor and City Council to consider the legislation, describing it as a “necessary and timely” evolution of the city’s approach to inclusivity. The commission said the legal framework “was largely built at a time when only a narrow definition of family and relationship was recognized.”
“As a result, many Seattle residents remain vulnerable to real and material harm,” the commission said.
The commission also pointed to multi-parent and multi-partner families, multi-generational households, chosen families, single parents, intentionally single individuals, and people in consensually nonmonogamous, asexual or aromantic relationships as groups that can face discrimination because their family structures fall outside traditional norms.
Seattle isn’t the first US city to recognize polyamory
Seattle would follow several other American cities that have adopted similar protections.
Somerville, Massachusetts, was the first U.S. city to formally recognize polyamorous relationships when it expanded its domestic partnership rules in 2020. The change extended certain benefits to poly partners, including hospital visitation rights and access to health insurance benefits.
In 2023, Somerville expanded its protections to specifically address discrimination in employment and interactions with police.
Portland, West Hollywood, Berkeley, Cambridge, Oakland, Olympia, Astoria and Hazel Park have also instituted similar protections, according to the report.
So while polygamy vs. polyamory can sound like a debate over terminology, Seattle’s proposal makes the practical distinction pretty clear: the city is considering protections for people in consensual multi-partner relationships and families, with the focus on preventing discrimination based on how those relationships are structured.
For anyone still mixing up the terms, that’s the key point to remember: polyamory and polygamy may both involve multiple partners, but Seattle’s proposed civil rights protections are specifically aimed at consensual relationship structures, not multiple-spouse marriage.
Source: Axios and NonMonogamyHelp

item.title: [Upworthy] People who got out of toxic relationships share the red flag they wish they'd taken seriously from the start
item.dc:creator: Adam Albright-Hanna; Upworthy Staff
item.description: There’s a particular kind of clarity that comes after leaving a bad relationship. Things that seemed explainable at the time suddenly line up into an obvious pattern. The warning was always there. It just didn’t look like a warning yet. Across social media thousands of people have shared the specific ‘red flag‘ moments they noticed early on but later regretted ignoring. The jokes that weren’t really jokes “Constantly ‘joking’ about other people being better looking or smarter,” wrote one person
item.content:encoded:
There’s a particular kind of clarity that comes after leaving a bad relationship. Things that seemed explainable at the time suddenly line up into an obvious pattern. The warning was always there. It just didn’t look like a warning yet.
Across social media thousands of people have shared the specific ‘red flag‘ moments they noticed early on but later regretted ignoring.
The jokes that weren’t really jokes
“Constantly ‘joking’ about other people being better looking or smarter,” wrote one person on Reddit. “At first, I brushed it off as humor, but over time it became clear that those ‘jokes’ were actually digs at my self-esteem. Should’ve realized earlier that a relationship where someone makes you feel less than isn’t healthy.” The camouflage of humor is one of the most common delivery mechanisms for contempt, it gives the person plausible deniability while the cumulative damage adds up.
The tip thief at the restaurant
“When we first started dating, we went to a restaurant, and he spotted the server’s tip on the table and pocketed the money with a smug look on his face,” one person shared with BuzzFeed. “He proceeded to do it to two of her tables.” She stayed. He turned out to be “broke, lazy, and entitled.” How someone treats a stranger, especially one who can’t push back, tends to be a more reliable window into their character than how they treat you when they’re trying to impress you.
The convenient indifference
“Being indifferent to everything,” wrote another Reddit user. “They do not want to give an opinion on anything or be a part of decision-making, no matter how major it is.” It can feel easygoing at first, low-maintenance, drama-free. What it often turns out to be is a way of remaining unaccountable. You can’t be blamed for outcomes you never weighed in on.
When the weirdness gets explained away
“His ex-wife showed up at one of our first dates and made a big scene,” shared one person on BuzzFeed. “He kept assuring me she was just having a hard time moving on.” She interrupted more dates, pranked the writer at work, and broke into their car. “He dumped me to go back to her. As people say, if it feels weird, IT IS WEIRD.”
The target of unspecified anger
From Bored Panda: “She was always angry with me about something. Some way that she felt mistreated, unseen, etc. It was so consistent that I realized it had nothing to do with me. She just needed someone to be the target of her anger, and I wasn’t interested in being that someone.” Chronic, diffuse anger that lands on you regardless of what you do isn’t about you, but staying in it is a choice that gets harder to reverse the longer you make it.
The gaslighting that didn’t look like gaslighting yet
“She would say that I was yelling when I wasn’t,” shared one person. “She would say I had said hurtful things and that I ‘don’t even realize what I was saying.’ I ended up seeing a psychiatrist at her suggestion and was put on medication for seven years.” The insidious thing about gaslighting is that it works precisely because the person experiencing it assumes the confusion is their fault. If you find yourself constantly questioning your own memory of conversations, that’s worth examining.
The love-bombing
Psychology Today notes that a 2021 Reddit survey on early warning signs of abusive relationships repeatedly surfaced one pattern: intensity that arrives too soon. “You’re the only one who understands me. I never met anyone like you before.” A whirlwind of attention and validation (like constant messages and declarations of connection after a few weeks) can feel like finally being truly seen. It can also be a way of establishing emotional debt before the dynamic shifts.
What people notice looking back on it
The most common thread across thousands of these accounts isn’t that the red flags were invisible. It’s that they were visible and felt in real time, but were talked out of taking them seriously by the other person and by the relationship’s good moments, or by the internal voice that says you’re being too sensitive, too suspicious, too demanding.
“If it feels weird, it is weird” is not a perfect heuristic. But checking in with that feeling, rather than immediately explaining it away, appears to be one of the more consistent pieces of advice from people who wish they’d done it sooner.
This article originally appeared in April. It has been updated.

item.content:encoded:
Your love horoscope for September 21, 2026, suggests you'll be more serious, more patient and more focused on long-term relationships. The Moon is in Capricorn, and Uttara Ashadha Nakshatra makes people loyal, self-respecting and able to make decisions that they can rely on. Single people may be choosier about who they hang with.
How to Navigate Today’s Energy
Let your actions say what words cannot. Capricorn energy wants to keep things the same, and Uttara Ashadha energy wants relationships that can handle stress and responsibility. Couples can talk about their future duties, finances, family plans or realistic expectations. Love is not a contract. Be nice. Singles need consistency more than charm. Today, those who follow plans, communicate well, and respect boundaries have greater potential.
Zodiac Signs That Need Care Today
Cancer: You could be craving more emotional warmth from someone who shows love through doing something for you. Don’t assume that they are less interested because they are less active. Notice what they are always doing for you.
Aries:
Your relationship may not be progressing as quickly as you wish. Don't try to rush people into commitment; it could backfire. Let people decide when they are ready, in their own time.
Libra: If you think something important is unfair, tell someone.
To find real balance, you both have to change.
Gemini:
When you talk about responsibility, it may weigh more heavily than you think. If someone asks you a serious question, don’t dodge it. Clear answers help prevent confusion in the future.
Zodiac Signs That May Enjoy Good Luck
Capricorn: You may look better if you act more mature today. Singles may like someone who values ambition and loyalty. Couples feel safer when they’ve reached an accord on a major future issue.
Taurus: Your relationship seems safe and calm. Reliability proves your partner cares, and singles are more likely to choose someone whose intentions become clearer over time.
Virgo: Attentive care for someone strengthens a good relationship. Your little daily actions may show someone how valuable you are, instead of big, showy displays of affection.
Scorpio: Trust may blossom quietly. You may learn more about how serious they are about the relationship through a private conversation, especially if they haven’t committed yet.
Balanced Day for These Zodiac Signs
Leo: You feel the same about them, but don't let pride stop you from making peace.
Sagittarius: You like your freedom, but you may have to work on a promise you have already made.
Aquarius: Emotions may develop slowly, putting the pragmatic compatibility of an individual to the test.
Pisces: If your expectations are grounded in reality, you may feel emotionally close to someone.
Lucky Action of the Day
Don't be late, don't forget something important, and don't break a promise.

item.description: The Challenge star CT Tamburello is revealing new details about his surprising romance with The Real Housewives of Atlanta’s Phaedra Parks. “I’ll say — I don’t want to jinx it — but I’ll say we’re in a good place,” CT, 46, exclusively told Us on Saturday, September 19, while walking the UFC 331 on Paramount+ red carpet outside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. item.content:encoded:
The Challenge star CT Tamburello is revealing new details about his surprising romance with The Real Housewives of Atlanta’s Phaedra Parks.
“I’ll say — I don’t want to jinx it — but I’ll say we’re in a good place,” CT, 46, exclusively told Us on Saturday, September 19, while walking the UFC 331 on Paramount+ red carpet outside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.
Phaedra, 52, shocked the Bravoverse and MTV world alike when she confirmed her once-platonic relationship with CT had turned romantic. The pair later made their red carpet couple debut while attending 2026 Creative Arts Emmys on September 5.
“It’s definitely the real deal, and they’re really smitten with each other,” a source exclusively shared with Us shortly after their romance went public. “They became really close on The Traitors, but CT never thought he actually had a chance with Phaedra.”
The couple met in 2023, while filming season 2 of Peacock’s hit reality show. Although the pair grabbed the attention of viewers with their palpable chemistry, which included Phaedra’s loving “castle daddy” nickname for CT, their platonic relationship didn’t evolve until recently.
“He always had a bit of a crush on her and was interested, but he really valued their friendship and never wanted to cross that line,” the source said. “After his marriage ended, he and Phaedra started talking a lot more, and their relationship naturally grew from there.” (CT and his estranged wife, Catalina White, got married in 2024. She filed for divorce in January but later requested to dismiss the motion. Months later, in June, CT filed his own petition, claiming the pair’s marriage “is irretrievably broken.”)
The source continued, “Most of their relationship has been long-distance so far, but they have made it work and travel to see each other.”
When speaking to Us on Saturday, CT opened up about the pair’s long-distance romance and why — for now — he thinks it’s the perfect setup.
“I know I’m crazy in my own right. It’s probably for the best if I’m not around her every day, to be honest,” CT dished. “But she’s amazing. She really is. The way I would describe it is like Paula Abdul, ‘Opposites Attract.’ You remember that old video? That’s us, you know?”
While the reality TV star is obviously giddy about his new romance, he told Us he has learned that some things are best kept secret.
“I mean, contrary to popular belief, I do learn,” he joked. “Maybe a slower learner, but I do learn, and some things are better left unsaid and I think oversharing can be a bad thing.”
One thing CT is willing to share, however, is the thing he appreciates the most about his new girlfriend.
“With her, she just brings peace,” he said. “It’s easy to just stay calm around her.”

item.title: [theprint.in] Dating app fatigue is real. It's doomscrolling for love
item.dc:creator: Insha Jalil Waziri
item.description: Love, they say, has many faces. Cruel, kind, manipulative; lately, though, love is artificial. As more and more people turn to chatbots for love or companionship, it does make one wonder: Is modern dating still a thing? With the dating app fatigue at an all-time high, lovers and despos worldwide are starting to question whether it is all really worth it. Online dating is a trial by fire, but going on dates has progressively started to feel like entering the frying pan. Perhaps that is where this
item.content:encoded:
Love, they say, has many faces. Cruel, kind, manipulative; lately, though, love is artificial. As more and more people turn to chatbots for love or companionship, it does make one wonder: Is modern dating still a thing?
With the dating app fatigue at an all-time high, lovers and despos worldwide are starting to question whether it is all really worth it. Online dating is a trial by fire, but going on dates has progressively started to feel like entering the frying pan.
Perhaps that is where this swipe stress has come from. We know the result: a charred residue of any chemistry.
The premise of dating apps is enticing; it’s what draws you in: meet the love of your life (or the night) from the comfort of your couch.
But after the hundredth “So what brings you here” message, you start to wonder: Is that it? The urge to swipe becomes more powerful than the promised reward. It’s doomscrolling for love.
So while there may be a lot of fish in the sea. Being on a dating app is like fishing in the Great Pacific Garbage Dump. Useless and disappointing.
A 2017 study from the University of Bath found that an average UK adult has one in 562 chances of finding love on any given day. I don’t have the math to back me up, but trust me, a decade later that figure stands at one in a thousand.
Also Read: Where is my romcom moment? Hollywood promised it would happen at 27
RIP dating apps
If you found the right person for you in the middle of this geopolitical shitstorm, you’re one of the lucky ones. Also, the exception, not the rule. Modern dating is death by a thousand cuts.
Nothing is ever as it seems online. AI images are a menace (Google even made an ad about catfishing through it). And everyone is either a blogger or some type of “maxxer”; worse still, they turn out to be a manosphere junkie. Please take your red pill and leave; this is a safe space.
But in the midst of all that is also an emerging belief: I am better off by myself. Women, especially, are choosing not to be pulled back into a vicious circle of toxic relationships, putting someone else’s needs before their own and having to answer and adhere to all of society’s expectations. The male loneliness epidemic is not a result of women saying “no”, but of them saying “not anymore.”
In fact, a recent Institute for Family Studies survey found that the number of single young men in the US has increased by almost 50 per cent since the 2000s. And honestly, nothing threatens civilisation more than a million lonely guys with bad Wi-Fi and too much free time.
But in the face of plenty, of course, we will reject the available. After all, what if the next batch of matches is even better? Some apps are trying to find a solution to this. The League only shows you a select number of profiles every day. Hinge only offers eight free likes per day. And unless you message your match within 24 hours on Bumble, be prepared to lose them forever.
The crack in the shiny armour of modern dating is clearer than ever. And uncertainty rules the dating apps. It’s the ultimate will they or won’t they?
They say, “modern love is a cruel endeavour,” and to that I say, no s**t, Sherlock.
Views are personal.

item.title: [fortune.com] Dating apps are trying to cure swiping fatigue with pickleball, trivia nights, and fewer chats | Fortune

item.description: After years of captivating users with endless swipes, dating apps are now trying to get people to put their phones down and find connection in the real world. item.content:encoded:
After years of captivating users with endless swipes, dating apps are now trying to get people to put their phones down and find connection in the real world.
Tinder, the pioneer of the dating swipe, is now one of the companies leading this expansion of IRL events. In March, the company introduced an Events feature in its app and hosted a pilot event for users in Los Angeles.
Since then, the feature has started to catch on, especially with younger people, said Tinder chief product officer Mark Kantor. The company since March has seen 71% of its Gen Z users in L.A. visit the Events feature on its app. Meanwhile, only 63% of users 25 and older engaged with it.
The company has now expanded the feature to 20 cities, mostly in the U.S. but also in Europe. The idea, Kantor told Fortune via email, is to shed the label of “dating event” and instead allow users to meet potential matches while doing something they already love like pickleball, trivia, or sauna and cold plunge sessions.
The company has partnered with several companies to facilitate these kinds of activities including City Pickle, Joust, and Othership.
“The activity gives people a natural starting point, and the shared experience takes some of the pressure out of meeting someone new,” he said.
Another established dating app company, Bumble, said it is also helping extend its reach beyond swipes and messages with events and activations. This year, the company has taken over bars across New York for singles mixers, hosted a rooftop party in Nashville, and held an event with Barstool Sports’ Tommy Smokes in Boston.
“IRL has been part of Bumble’s DNA from the start. We know that one of the biggest points of friction in dating today is the gap between connecting online and actually meeting in person, and we’re focused on helping close that gap,” a Bumble spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.
Outside of dating apps, Gen Z and other young people have increasingly turned to in-person activities like run clubs for a sense of community, and also for romantic connection. According to Strava, participation in run clubs grew 59% over the past two years. At the same time, Gen Z is drinking less alcohol at bars and clubs, to the dismay of the night life industry.
Dating app companies’ increasing push for real-world events comes as user numbers have fallen.
Tinder’s daily active users were down 4% year over year in the second quarter, which was a slight improvement compared to past quarters. Paying Tinder users fell to 8.5 million as of the second quarter, an 11.5% drop compared to the same period two years earlier.
Bumble has experienced a steeper decline, with total paying users falling to 3.2 million in the second quarter from 4.1 million two years earlier—a 24% drop.
Swipe fatigue
Partly to blame for these declines may be swipe fatigue. A study of nearly 9,000 respondents from reverse lookup company Clarity Check in July found that 58% of respondents had deleted a dating app because they found it “emotionally draining.” Another 44% said they would prefer to meet someone in a low-pressure setting rather than get to know them through a profile.
Breeze, a dating app based in Delft, Netherlands, was created explicitly to get people to meet rather than swipe. The company, which has a team of 41 and has raised about $7 million in funding, charges by date rather than subscription.
Each user receives only a handful of profiles each day. If two people match, they fill out their availability rather than opening a chat, and then Breeze brings the pair together at a partner venue.
“A short real-world date tells you more about compatibility than weeks of texting, and it does it faster and with less of the anxiety and second-guessing that endless chat creates,” Marco van der Woude, Breeze’s cofounder and head of business development, told Fortune in an email.

item.title: [The News International] Gwyneth Paltrow unveils why she called Chris Martin divorce 'conscious uncoupling'
item.dc:creator: Maliha Javed
item.description: Gwyneth Paltrow unveils why she called Chris Martin divorce 'conscious uncoupling' Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin welcomed two kids, daughter Apple and son Moses Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin planned to "stay a family" after they parted ways. The actress and the Coldplay frontman caused a stir back in 2014 when they first described their divorce as "conscious uncoupling.” Now, the Marty Supreme star has described why they used the term and how they wanted to separate as smoothly as possible
item.content:encoded:
Gwyneth Paltrow unveils why she called Chris Martin divorce 'conscious uncoupling'
Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin welcomed two kids, daughter Apple and son Moses
Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin planned to "stay a family" after they parted ways.
The actress and the Coldplay frontman caused a stir back in 2014 when they first described their divorce as "conscious uncoupling.”
Now, the Marty Supreme star has described why they used the term and how they wanted to separate as smoothly as possible for their kids, daughter Apple Martin and son Moses.
“We really sat down and thought, like, is there a way that we could do this?" she said on the Friends Keep Secrets podcast.
She continued, “I talked to all my friends who came from a divorced household and I said, ‘Tell me what was the worst thing? Like, what do you feel you have scars from to this day?’”
Gwyneth admitted she was shocked to discover the problem was not the divorce but the challenges kids face growing up amid friction between parents.
The mom of two noted, “They said the worst part was like my parents, you know, my dad used to drop me off at the end of the driveway. Like it was so tense at my birthday parties, you know, they never ate dinner in the same room until my college graduation, and it caused me so much pain. So I was like, how could we not do that?”
So Gwyneth wanted her kids to grow up in a situation where “you’re all having dinner at the same table” no matter what.
She recalled, “So Chris and I had this therapist that was really brilliant, and he sort of introduced us to the concept and we just made a commitment to really put the kids first and so what that meant was to stay a family even though we weren’t a couple."
It is pertinent to mention that Gwyneth is now married to Brad Falchuk

item.title: [The Mercury News] Dear Abby: The neighbors’ kid disrupted movie night, and I don’t like their solution
item.dc:creator: Abigail Van Buren
item.description: DEAR ABBY: I am a single woman in a friendly neighborhood. Every month, I have the neighbors over for dinner and a movie. I like to be inclusive — bring the kids, bring the dogs! One couple recently had their elderly mom move in, and I installed a ramp so she could join us. Babies cry, dogs bark, women breastfeed, and all are welcome. I put sleeping bags on the floor for the kids to sit on while grownups sit on the couches. Cleanup is a bear, but every squished meatball on the floor reminds me h
item.content:encoded:
DEAR ABBY: I am a single woman in a friendly neighborhood. Every month, I have the neighbors over for dinner and a movie.
I like to be inclusive — bring the kids, bring the dogs! One couple recently had their elderly mom move in, and I installed a ramp so she could join us. Babies cry, dogs bark, women breastfeed, and all are welcome. I put sleeping bags on the floor for the kids to sit on while grownups sit on the couches.
Cleanup is a bear, but every squished meatball on the floor reminds me how much I love everyone.
Recently, a new couple moved in, so of course I invited them and their 6-year-old to join us. They warned me that he has severe autism, but I told them everyone is welcome, that he wouldn’t be expected to be quiet and that the house is thoroughly kid-proofed.
When the family showed up to join us, their child was horrible, even by my nonexistent standards for kiddo behavior. He screamed, threw food, bit, spit and hit the other kids and the dogs for an hour. Finally, everyone started to leave before the movie was over.
The boy’s parents really did try their best, and I was genuinely sympathetic.
They apologized the next day and said that if they were welcome in the future, they would alternate one parent staying home with their son while the other joined us. That sounds reasonable, but I don’t like it. I can’t be inclusive just when it suits me.
They have since invited me to their home for dinner, and their son was just as bad there, banishing my thoughts that maybe it was just a strange house he was reacting to.
I don’t know what to do with all this. I’m looking for a magic wand. Any suggestions?
— NEIGHBORLY IN THE EAST
DEAR NEIGHBORLY: You are a caring, lovely person, but there is no magic wand that will make that child’s severe autism and behavior problems go away.
Because you are determined to entertain the entire family, the practical solution would be to invite them and their son over on another evening when other children and pets won’t be at risk of injury. Your movie night will be history if it is disrupted like that again.
While I commend you for wanting to befriend the family, I think the parents had the right solution.
DEAR ABBY: I’m 70 now, and many of my friends and family spend our time together complaining about their various ailments.
I, too, have had some problems but do not make them a part of our visits unless I’m asked about them.
How can I rethink how to make these times more positive for everyone involved?
— POSITIVE IN OREGON
DEAR POSITIVE: Sometimes, people of a certain age talk about their health problems because they have become less active and can find little else to talk about. To keep the energy flowing in a more positive direction, help your friends find hobbies and other interests to discuss.
Even if they have medical issues, most people can manage quiet activities like board games, card games, a book club or a knitting circle. If all else fails, you can always ask them about their families as a change of subject.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips wrote this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

item.content:encoded:
Weekly Love Horoscopes For September 21 - 27 — Libra Season Starts
The weekly love horoscope for September 21 to 27, 2026 shows a great week for every zodiac sign's relationship, although the weekend looks a little dicey. Monday is a great day for getting together with someone special or socializing because the Sun sextiles Jupiter on September 21, a light and upbeat type of energy, which is a great way to start the week.
The Sun enters Libra on September 22. During Libra season, people are usually more focused on love and social activities than usual. When Mars begins its transit through Leo on September 27, prepare to feel more confident in yourself and eager to get out and about. The weekend has potential for things to go south because you may question your feelings for someone as the Sun opposes Neptune on Friday and becomes part of the Full Moon energy on the 26th. It'll be easy to default to thinking about the worst-case scenario, but try looking at things from a different perspective to avoid crashing out. The energy will soon pass.
Weekly love horoscopes for September 21 to 27, 2026:
Aries
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
This week represents a turning point in your love life. The Sun’s opposition to Neptune will likely make you question a close relationship on Friday.
It is time to look at how your relationship is working, Aries. Or if you're single and looking, think about what your next step is. Choose the path of creativity and compassion over suspicion and mistrust if you can.
Taurus
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Venus is transiting through your 7th house of partners and is in its shadow period energy before it turns retrograde in October. That means you can expect to be deep in contemplation about your relationship this week.
The Full Moon and the Sun’s opposition to Neptune hits your 12th house of the subconscious this weekend. This will help you decide if you are with the right person, Taurus. It could also bring up issues and anger relating to past relationships. Do your best not to project.
Gemini
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
On September 22, the Sun’s entrance into Libra lights up your 5th house of love and romance. This is just the start of an entire astrological month of good times, Gemini.
On Saturday, the Aries Full Moon lights up the part of your chart dealing with friends and your social life. This is a weekend you'll want to spend with those who align with you mentally and emotionally.
Cancer
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Venus is transiting your 5th house of love, which is significant for your relationships. Including your relationship with yourself, Cancer!
Since Venus is getting closer to its retrograde phase, expect to start thinking about how you can bring some more romance into your relationship, especially if you've been with someone for a while.
I wouldn't be surprised if the Aries Full Moon triggers a conflict between your business and personal life at the end of the week. You may feel pulled in different directions. Hidden issues or resentments can erupt, so it’s important to maintain a clear head and not get lost in Neptune’s fog.
Leo
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
It's a relatively quiet week for your love life, Leo. But no news is usually good news when it comes to astrology.
This weekend, the Sun’s opposition to Neptune lights up your 3rd house of communication and your 9th house of philosophy, learning, and travel. This is also where the Full Moon falls on Saturday, which tells me there is potential for travel or meeting someone who lives at a distance.
One thing I do see happening for you this week is a change of perspective.
Virgo
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
The Sun’s opposition to Neptune this week offers a glimpse into your personal self-esteem. The way you feel about yourself often dictates who you allow into your life, Virgo.
Saturday's Full Moon in Aries falls in your 8th house, which rules things like intimacy and money. This energy represents a transformation, so you may find yourself at a turning point in love this weekend.
Libra
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Your birthday season has officially begun! The Sun-Neptune opposition this week will shed light on a current love interest or someone you would like to know better and how they are impacting your life.
On Saturday, the Full Moon lights up your partnership sector. While it may not be all fireworks right now, some reflection and simple appreciation of the small things lead to very positive results for you this week, Libra.
Scorpio
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Your magnetism and intensity are at an all-time high with Venus transiting through your 1st house. If you don't feel attractive and emboldened this week, I'd be very surprised.
Scorpio, keep that same energy this weekend because if you have been idolizing someone, prepare for the Full Moon to bring you back down to earth. This doesn’t mean an ending is inevitable, but it does mean you may have to adjust your expectations a bit.
Sagittarius
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
You may crave a far-away adventure and even make plans for one this week. But hey, what else is new?
The Full Moon lands in your 5th house of love this weekend. If things in a relationship seem different or not as fiery as you are used to, use this moon to reflect on whether or not you are truly aligned with your love interest or person of interest.
Capricorn
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
This is the last week of Mars transiting your 7th house of partners. Once the planet of passion enters Leo, your 8th house, next week, things might not feel as exciting, so enjoy it while you can!
On Saturday, the Full Moon falls in your 4th house, which rules your foundation in life. This is a good weekend to really soak in the beauty in those around you. Don’t get drawn into negative emotions or game-playing, Capricorn.
Aquarius
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
This is actually a great week for your love life, Aquarius. You're about to reach a turning point for the better as past tensions make way for a more balanced outlook.
The Aries Full Moon falls in your 3rd house on Saturday, making you feel more social and talkative this weekend. I think you're ready for a short adventure.
Pisces
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
The Sun leaves your 7th house of partners on Tuesday and enters your 8th house, which is far deeper and more profound energy.
Venus is transiting through Scorpio, which is a complementary sign for you. You may be interested in someone who lives at a distance or even in another country.
Over the weekend, the Aries moon sheds light on the condition of your personal self-worth and how this affects your romantic choices for better or worse.
Leslie Hale is a professional astrologer with over 30 years of experience specializing in astrological guidance to empower you with knowledge of future events, relationships, finances, and major life situations.

item.title: [The i Paper] I'm having a quasi affair // micro cheating on husband
item.dc:creator: Anonymous

item.content:encoded:
“Micro cheating” is a bit slippery to define. In my parents’ day, in the 1980s, I imagine it would be removing your wedding ring when you attended a drinks party. Or failing to mention that you have a husband when someone offers to buy you a baby-cham at the bar. Nowadays there are many ways to micro-cheat with WhatsApp and social media, making it easier than ever.
A term popularised by the dating coach Melanie Schilling in 2017, micro cheating isn’t a one size fits all. What does and doesn’t count feels individual and varies between couples (is liking someone else’ s Instagram photos micro cheating?) I’d personally define it as the things you do or say which you know would upset your partner if they knew. A survey found 40 per cent of Brits believe that “developing any romantic feelings [even] without acting on them” is cheating. So perhaps calling it “micro” is just an attempt to make it sound less terrible than it really is.
The problem is: I think if most married couples were honest, they’d admit that they’ve thought that way about other people, and fantasised about sleeping with them. I’m not proud of it but I have been micro-cheating on my husband for 18 months.
Shorts
I’m 48 and have been married to Simon* for 22 years. We have two teenage boys. Simon is wedded to his work and we get on well, but I feel like we’re ships in the night. We spend too long on our laptops. We talk about how we need to prioritise one another but we’re too busy. We have stressful jobs, and at the end of the day, we tend to stare at our phones. Perimenopause hasn’t helped much either. I don’t fancy Simon and feel angry a lot.
A year and a half ago, I met Dean at a health and wellness conference in Corfu. I work in corporate hospitality and we were staying at a beautiful luxury hotel. Each day we’d attend talks about the ‘future of hospitality’, which was boring, but at 5pm everyone would meet for drinks.
On the second night of the conference, Dean and I ended up sitting together at the local taverna. He was Irish, in his late 40s, recently divorced and worked in PR. He lived in Bali, not the UK. I remember noticing him right away; he was good-looking, but I also dismissed him as annoying. He kept name-dropping famous people that he’d worked with.
Then after a while, perhaps influenced by three glasses of wine, we got chatting. We had a lot in common. We loved 90s dance music. We’d gone clubbing to the same places in our youth. We loved the same films – any Steve Martin comedy. I realised that talking about this stuff was something I missed. Simon and I were in functional parent mode; we talked about what to eat for tea and whether the boys were going to fail their exams.
Dean and I got drunk and we swapped numbers. I felt 18, like I was in this fantasy where I was desirable again. To be honest, I didn’t think I fancied people anymore until I met Dean.
When I woke up the following day, I felt guilty. Why had I found it so easy to give Dean my number? I told myself he would be a “useful work contact”, and vowed to give him a wide berth. On the second night, however, when I was sitting at the bar, quite drunk yet again (I was letting my hair down; I might even have been smoking too…), I got a text from Dean. “I was hoping we could meet up. Fancy coming to my room for a nightcap?”
To be honest, I was stunned. I’d not seen him all day and thought he’d been flirting with me the night before because a lot of people in our industry can be super friendly. I told him that I’d give it a miss. Then he sent another text saying he was disappointed – “I thought we had chemistry,” he said.
At that point I should have fully shut it down but instead I typed: “I really like you. I would love to come to your room but I can’t do it as I know what will happen. I’m sorry.” The reality was that because I was away on my own, in a different country, I felt like I should have a holiday fling!
I fell asleep and the next day got a text from Dean saying that he was leaving early as he had to go home for a work meeting. I felt flat, like I’d missed an opportunity. If I’d slept with Dean, then probably the whole thing would have finished right there. But instead, that’s when we started messaging one another in earnest.
We used Instagram messenger, not WhatsApp – where I text most people. I’ve never actually texted a man who wasn’t Simon, not romantically at least and to begin with I was disoriented. Sometimes Dean would text about work-related things. So he’d be sharing a client and then he would be telling me that he was feeling sad because he’d injured his knee.
He would send me selfies and photos of everything in his life. Not naked ones, but just a diary showing what he was doing. We messaged a lot. It was a running conversation that we picked up as soon as we were both online. I started putting kisses at the end of each message. I also confided in him about feeling lonely.
It felt like cheating because I don’t usually put kisses at the end of messages. Also, I was finding that Dean was cropping up more often in my mind, and I’d wonder what he was up to. But he was also so far away that it felt safe. We didn’t have to take anything further, and Simon didn’t have to find out.
At other times I convinced myself it wasn’t cheating as Dean would share information about a woman he was seeing. Weirdly, I felt hurt but knew I couldn’t – I’m married!
The life that Dean was living seemed idyllic and a long way away from me putting washing in the machine and avoiding Simon, who was often in a permanent sulk. I should have felt guiltier, but as the weeks passed, I justified it because I was feeling low. Our marriage had deteriorated. I was comparing Simon to Dean and Dean was just a fantasy. But it felt strangely intimate too. He’d share songs that we both loved. I found myself getting obsessive. I knew it was ridiculous. Months passed and each morning I’d wait for a message, feeling disappointed if there was nothing there.
Simon was now working every hour of the day; I mean, I assumed he was. I would regularly delete the chats with Dean but Simon has never been one to check my phone. One time my son Aidan picked it up and I hadn’t deleted the conversation. He said: “Who is this dude?” I blushed. “He’s just a work friend. We message about work stuff,” I’d said. Luckily, he didn’t mention it again.
When I spoke to female friends, they were aghast. Why was I bothering to text this guy who lived so far away? What was his agenda? Money? Did he have any intention of meeting up with me? What was I getting out of the whole thing? It was hard to explain. I was getting friendship, and a bit of flirtation thrown in for good measure.
With micro-cheating, you get “micro-doses” of guilt. I justified it because I was bored. Because Simon and I didn’t have sex. Because I felt old and like time was running out. The truth was that I felt closer to Dean than to Simon after 12 months of texting. We knew each other really well.
He would often say things like “if we’d met back in the 90s, we would have been an item.” But he never made plans to come to the UK, even though I knew that he could. There were times when I tried to push things, suggesting that perhaps I should come to Bali. I increasingly felt like my feelings were much stronger than his.
Then one morning a couple of months ago, when I was getting ready to drive to the garden centre, I checked my phone and Dean had sent me a photo of his penis! I felt like perhaps he’d sent it by mistake. Luckily, it disappeared as Instagram has a one-view feature. “I’m sorry,” Dean texted later. I felt so mixed about it. I did fancy him. I sometimes thought about what it would be like. I dreamt about it, in fact.
The photo did feel like a line had been crossed. I also felt like he was maybe playing me; if I didn’t message for a few days, he’d double down and send me a long voice note. I’d hear his voice, immediately felt closer and more obsessive again.
But the photo made me decide to go cold turkey. I blocked him – of course there was no resolution because we didn’t have a relationship in the first place but I felt like I was going mad. Then, after two weeks, I unblocked him and messaged. “I can’t stop thinking about you. How’s work?” I knew it was stupid. That was last month.
I know I have to put energy into my marriage but I feel so over it. The energy I get from Dean makes me feel alive. Today I am still “micro cheating”. Except it doesn’t feel quite so micro anymore. It feels like a massive lie because it’s been going on so long. I keep telling myself it’s pointless. That I am betraying Simon. That I owe it to my sons to give it up and make more of an effort at home. There are days when I feel Dean and I will meet up in real life and others when I think he’s stringing a whole host of women along.
He’s an enigma in many ways. The opposite of the man I’ve shared a bed with for so many years. I know that I’m wasting time. But I’m also totally addicted. I sometimes daydream a scenario where we meet. I also know that if we did meet, there’d be too much pressure on the whole thing, as my expectations of him are way too high. I have sort of made him into an ideal partner, filled in the blanks and ensured he has all the things I look for. He’d never be able to live up to that high standard anyway.

item.content:encoded:
Dear Abby | Good neighbor learns inclusivity has limits
Today's advice from Dear Abby.
DEAR ABBY: I am a single woman in a friendly neighborhood. Every month, I have the neighbors over for dinner and a movie. I like to be inclusive — bring the kids, bring the dogs! One couple recently had their elderly mom move in, and I installed a ramp so she could join us. Babies cry, dogs bark, women breastfeed, but all are welcome. I put sleeping bags on the floor for the kids to sit on while grownups sit on the couches. Cleanup is a bear, but every squished meatball on the floor reminds me how much I love everyone.
Recently, a new couple moved in, so of course I invited them and their 6-year-old to join us. They warned me that he has severe autism, but I told them everyone is welcome, that he wouldn’t be expected to be quiet and that the house is thoroughly kid-proofed. When the family showed up to join us, their child was horrible, even by my nonexistent standards for kiddo behavior. He screamed, threw food, bit, spit and hit the other kids and the dogs for an hour. Finally, everyone started to leave before the movie was over. The boy’s parents really did try their best, and I was genuinely sympathetic. They apologized the next day and said that if they were welcome in the future, they would alternate one parent staying home with their son while the other joined us. That sounds reasonable, but I don’t like it. I can’t be inclusive just when it suits me. They have since invited me to their home for dinner, and their son was just as bad there, banishing my thoughts that maybe it was just a strange house he was reacting to. I don’t know what to do with all this. I’m looking for a magic wand. Any suggestions?
— NEIGHBORLY IN THE EAST
DEAR NEIGHBORLY: You are a caring, lovely person, but there is no magic wand that will make that child’s severe autism and behavior problems go away. Because you are determined to entertain the entire family, the practical solution would be to invite them and their son over on another evening when other children and pets won’t be at risk of injury. Your movie night will be history if it is disrupted like that again. While I commend you for wanting to befriend the family, I think the parents had the right solution.
** ** **
DEAR ABBY: I’m 70 now, and many of my friends and family spend our time together complaining about their various ailments. I, too, have had some problems but do not make them a part of our visits unless I’m asked about them. How can I rethink how to make these times more positive for everyone involved?
— POSITIVE IN OREGON
DEAR POSITIVE: Sometimes, people of a certain age talk about their health problems because they have become less active and can find little else to talk about. To keep the energy flowing in a more positive direction, help your friends find hobbies and other interests to discuss. Even if they have medical issues, most people can manage quiet activities like board games, card games, a book club or a knitting circle. If all else fails, you can always ask them about their families as a change of subject.
