item.content:encoded:
Justine (L’amour est dans le pré) interrompt brusquement son speed dating avec Audran : “Je ne peux pas rester”

Lors du nouvel épisode de L’amour est dans le pré, diffusé ce lundi 14 septembre sur M6, Justine a rencontré ses prétendants. Alors qu’elle faisait la connaissance d’Audran, la jeune femme ne s’est pas sentie bien et a soudainement quitté la péniche.

Un moment pour le moins mouvementé. Après Vincent, son ami de longue date, Justine a pu se lancer dans l’étape des speed datings. Lors du nouvel épisode de L’amour est dans le pré, diffusé ce lundi 14 septembre sur M6, la jeune femme de 34 ans a donné rendez-vous à cinq prétendants sur la péniche Quai Liberté à Liberté. Dépanneur automobile de 27 ans, Audran a été le premier à se lancer dans le bain. Alors qu’il dévoilait les raisons qui l’ont poussé à écrire à la pétillante propriétaire d’une ferme pédagogique, cette dernière a rapidement coupé court à leur échange. «Attends, ne bouge pas. Je ne peux pas rester sur le bateau», a-t-elle lancé, avant de prendre la fuite. Une situation qui a laissé sans voix Karine Le Marchand, qui suivait avec attention ce premier tête-à-tête au côté de Vincent. «Elle est partie !» Face à la surprise de l’animatrice, l’apiculteur a indiqué que Justine a «le mal de mer».

Bien que n’étant pas au meilleur de sa forme, la candidate s’est empressée de retrouver Audran pour poursuivre leur discussion. «Je suis désolée. Est-ce que tu peux te mettre en face comme ça, je ne vois pas l’eau qui est derrière toi», lui a-t-elle demandé, avant de le rassurer : «C’est une horreur mais c’est bon. C’est hyper mal poli, je suis désolée.» Alors qu’elle tentait de reprendre le fil de la conversation, Justine s’est une nouvelle fois éclipsée pour prendre l’air, laissant seul son soupirant. «Le pauvre. C’est la catastrophe. Ce n’est jamais arrivé dans toute l’histoire de L’amour est dans le pré !», a-t-elle indiqué avant de mettre fin à ces dix minutes interminables de speed dating. Si Audran était satisfait de cette rencontre, il en a été tout autre pour Justine.

Passer la publicité

Justine (L’amour est dans le pré) déçue par sa rencontre avec Audran : “Le problème, c’est sa taille”

À l’issue de cet «entretien historique», Karine Le Marchand s’est empressée de retrouver Justine pour un petit débriefing. Dès l’arrivée de la mère d’Alya, la candidate est revenue sur son malaise mais aussi sur un détail qui l’a quelque peu déçu. Si elle souhaite rencontrer un homme aussi grand qu’elle, Audran ne répond malheureusement pas à ce critère. «Le problème, c’est sa taille», a-t-elle avoué, avant d’être coupée net par la présentatrice : «Mais à quel moment on parle on parle de la taille d’un mec ? Là, tu nous l’as castré pour les 30 prochaines années !»

Après cette remarque, le constat a été sans appel pour Justine. «Je lui ai fait le pire date de sa vie». Pour éviter que ce scénario ne se reproduise, Karine Le Marchand lui a proposé d’installer une table dehors. Une suggestion que la principale intéressée a préféré décliner, au grand dam de la présentatrice. Reste à savoir si la suite des speed datings sera aussi chaotique.

item.title: [Awards Buzz] TIFF: ‘In Waves’ is a Beautiful Animated Tale of Deep Connection
item.dc:creator: Abe Friedtanzer
item.description: Is it better to live without the knowledge that the end might come soon, savoring every moment in the process, or to enjoy a more carefree existence where the time, moment, and circumstance of death is never considered? Having a terminal or incurable disease can affect the way a person approaches every opportunity and relationship, creating the opportunity for tremendous appreciation of things that might otherwise not seem momentous and also inviting the potential for a great deal of heartbreak.
item.content:encoded:
Is it better to live without the knowledge that the end might come soon, savoring every moment in the process, or to enjoy a more carefree existence where the time, moment, and circumstance of death is never considered? Having a terminal or incurable disease can affect the way a person approaches every opportunity and relationship, creating the opportunity for tremendous appreciation of things that might otherwise not seem momentous and also inviting the potential for a great deal of heartbreak. In Waves chooses to emphasize the positive in its tender love story set against backdrop of the vast, beautiful ocean.
AJ and Kristen each have their separate passions – he skateboards and she surfs. When they meet, they quickly become close and realize their feelings for each other. When Kristen is diagnosed with cancer, the limits of what previously seemed like a boundless romance begin to weigh on them. Despite the uncertainty of whether they’ll be able to spend a long life together, they forge ahead to create lasting moments of connection, even if they’re not always on the same page about what’s meaningful and what they each need to ensure that they don’t get too hurt along the way.
This animated film is based on the 2019 graphic novel of the same name by AJ Dungo, based on his own experiences losing a partner. Phuong Mai Nguyen makes an assured feature directorial debut with a sensitive and moving depiction of instant, poignant chemistry and the way in which riding a surfboard and feeling attuned to the water adds such a degree of warmth and magic to each moment. The ocean has rarely felt as vivid or three-dimensional as it does here, leaping off the screen to convey its temperature, glow, and sparkle.
This is largely a two-person story, though other characters figure into the storyline, including friends and family members who come and go as they two navigate a difficult journey together and apart. Will Sharpe and Stephanie Hsu prove to be excellent choices to voice AJ and Kristen, both adept at comedy with recent TV roles on Too Much and Laid, respectively, and experienced in more subtle genre fusion with award-nominated performances in The White Lotus and Everything Everywhere All at Once. These roles feel more serious but still full of personality, and Sharpe and Hsu embody them well.
Animation offers a wonderful canvas through which to explore the notion of grief, and AJ’s passion for drawing also figures in significantly, as this film’s graphic novel basis indicates. To adapt this in live-action wouldn’t feel nearly as creative or fitting, and it’s also a film that, due to its Netflix release, will likely be seen mostly by audiences on their home screens, an experience that should still be just as rewarding as watching in a theater. This is a story with beauty embedded within its narrative that feels just as potent in its visual presentation.
In Waves is a film that finds a (relatively) comfortable and accessible way to engage with notions of grief and loss, and the way in which people consider how close they can get when they know that something isn’t going to last forever. There’s a real sincerity that comes across from its straightforward presentation and then the magical way in which images and memories are preserved through drawings and the sound of the ocean. In Waves is a film that, like its protagonist for her partner, lingers long after the credits roll, able to capture something that can feel fleeting but is far more resilient and lasting.
Movie Rating: 8/10
In Waves makes its international premiere in the Discovery section at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival and will be released on Netflix on December 11th.

item.title: [Psychology Today] Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness
item.dc:creator: Eugene Beresin M D; M A
item.description:
Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness The role of secure attachment in preventing loneliness and misuse of social media.
Posted September 14, 2026 Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D. Key points - Secure attachments are essential for cognitive, social, and emotional well-being. - Secure attachments prevent loneliness in young people by fostering bonding with others and social skills. - Research shows that secure attachments help prevent social media addiction and digital media
item.content:encoded:
Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness
The role of secure attachment in preventing loneliness and misuse of social media.

Posted September 14, 2026 Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
Key points
- Secure attachments are essential for cognitive, social, and emotional well-being.
- Secure attachments prevent loneliness in young people by fostering bonding with others and social skills.
- Research shows that secure attachments help prevent social media addiction and digital media misuse.
- Parents can learn skills for establishing secure attachments in early life and throught the life cycle.
All the lonely people/Where do they all come from/All the lonely people/Where do they all belong
Lennon and McCartney
With Gen Z now reporting the highest rates of loneliness of any generation, and parents more concerned than ever about the perils of social media amid recent suits against META, researchers and clinicians are increasingly pointing to something we’ve understood for decades: the power of a secure, trusting bond between a child and the adults who raise them.
In the psychological literature, they appear to be crucial for:
- Effective and accurate cognitive functions
- Emotional flexibility
- Feeling safer and more secure
- Finding meaning in experiences
- Self-regulation and managing one’s own feelings and behaviors
- The capacity for intimacy and healthy interpersonal relationships
- Empathy
- Self-awareness and comfort with one’s identity
- Resilience
That’s a lot, and more than any parent or caregiver could possibly want for our kids, teens, and young adults. Kids with secure attachments tend to handle stress better, bounce back from setbacks, form closer friendships, and know themselves more clearly.
But how does this happen?
We humans are pack animals. We need each other. We need relationships.
As Winnicott so clearly pointed out, development requires both a biological endowment and a facilitating environment. The former is rooted in genetics and physical contributions to our development, and the second, perhaps most important part of our life experience, is rooted in relationships.
Dan Siegel summarized the process well. It is a gradual process, beginning and grounded in the first three years of life. Its components include:
- Collaborative Communication: Parental attunement to the child
- Reflective Dialogue: Creating the sense that subjective experience is important and can be shared. This allows the child to be seen
- Repair: Identification and repair of miscommunications and misunderstandings. This requires that both parent and child are mindful of breaches, and use apology and reparations, to mend fences
- Emotional Communication: Sharing and amplifying the positive and mitigating the negative in the interpersonal world of parent and child
- Developing Coherent Narratives: Helping the child and teen develop an internal autobiographical sense of self, and self-awareness, key for self-reflection and a solid sense of identity
Attachment theory has shaped how we understand social and emotional development, parenting, and our own relational patterns. Yet little research addresses how secure attachment protects against specific, longstanding threats to youth development.
In particular, let’s consider loneliness and misuse of social media.
Secure Attachment and Loneliness
On May 3, 2023, The United States Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy released a new Advisory calling attention to the public health crisis of loneliness, isolation, and lack of connection in our country.
According to the Advisory, social connection is a critical but underappreciated contributor to individual overall health, community safety, and resilience. Yet, around half of all U.S. adults report experiencing loneliness, with some of the highest rates among our young people. In fact, today the Gen Z population reports the highest rates of loneliness.
The Surgeon General noted that it is important to “Invest in your relationship with your child or loved one by recognizing that strong, secure attachments are protective and a good foundation for other healthy relationships.”
The report didn’t specify how to foster these attachments (practical examples follow below.) There have been some studies (though few) on how secure attachment mitigates loneliness.
Consider a teenager who gets left out of a group chat, or shows up to find plans have changed without them. A securely attached teen is more likely to mention it to a parent that night, or reach out to another friend, rather than sitting with it alone and assuming the worst about themselves.
Teenagers’ needs for bonding with others, feeling fulfilled, and trust are grounded in their secure attachment profile. As such, they are more likely to seek help and support when distressed, rather than worrying alone. Their sense of connection to others also helps them build highly developed social skills, mitigating temporary isolation without it developing into chronic loneliness. Their sense of connection becomes a part of their autobiographical narrative, and is an important outcome of secure attachment.
Secure Attachment and Problematic Social Media Use
Parents, caregivers, clinicians, and legislators alike have grown concerned about digital media because of both its habit-forming design, and the way young people can misuse it, for instance, for bullying, excessive texting, or ghosting.
Though research is limited, evidence suggests that secure attachments reduce vulnerability to digital media misuse. One study linked insecure attachment to social media addiction, with social support outside of media use acting as a mediator. Another study found secure attachment associated with less addiction and fewer mental health problems.
Secure attachments can reduce a young person’s need to look to social media for validation, emotional regulation, and relief from negative emotions.
None of this means social media is inherently harmful—for many young people, it’s a genuine source of connection and community. The point is more specific: When a young person already feels secure and connected, they’re less likely to depend on a device to meet needs the device can’t fulfill.
What Can Parents and Caregivers Do
With Siegel’s framework in mind, here are some guidelines for nurturing secure attachment:
- When your child is upset, slow down, get on their level, name their feelings, and match your tone before jumping to solutions.
- Ask an open question about their day, and sit with the whole answer with curiosity, instead of moving straight to advice.
- After a blowup, come back later and name what happened. You might say, “I got too frustrated earlier, and I’m sorry” or something similar. The repair matters more than the rupture.
- Identify and name positive moments aloud in the moment they happen so the good moments register. This could look like, “I love that we laughed about that together,” or “I enjoyed watching that with you.”
- To facilitate narrative building skills, ask your teen to tell you about their day as a story instead of a checklist. For example, try phrases like, “Walk me through your day,” as opposed to “How was school.”
Promoting secure attachments is not easy. For many, Siegel’s skills are complicated by real obstacles: parents’ own insecure attachment histories; adverse childhood experiences; economic pressure; disparities related to race, immigration status, or gender identity; unstable family structure; domestic conflict; or psychiatric or physical disability.
It is imperative to recognize these obstacles and seek support — from family, friends, spiritual leaders, or mental health professionals.
And in the process of getting help, parents and caregivers may not only promote secure attachments with their children but earn secure attachment profiles for themselves.
To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
Also posted in a longer form at the Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds at Massachusetts General Hospital.
References
Siegel, D. J. (1999). The developing mind: Toward a neurobiology of interpersonal experience. Guilford Press.
Office of the Surgeon General (OSG). Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on the Healing Effects of Social Connection and Community [Internet]. Washington (DC): US Department of Health and Human Services; 2023–. PMID: 37792968.
Office of the Surgeon General (OSG). Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory [Internet]. Washington (DC): US Department of Health and Human Services; 2023. PMID: 37721985.
Eichenberg et al. BMC Psychiatry (2024) 24:278. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-024-05709-z
Winnicott DW. The Maturational Processes and the Facilitating Environment. New York: International Universities Press, 1965.

item.content:encoded:
L’Amour est dans le pré 2026 : “Ça m’a vraiment déçue !” Pourquoi Justine a très mal vécu son speed-dating ?

Publié le Par Drifa Maza

Ce lundi 14 septembre 2026, Justine sera au cœur de l’intrigue amoureuse dans L’Amour est dans le pré, diffusée sur M6. Toutefois, la candidate n’a pas exactement vécu l’aventure à laquelle elle s’attendait. Pourquoi l’étape du speed dating a-t-elle été compliquée pour elle ? Elle s’est confiée sur ses péripéties, plusieurs mois après le tournage.

Depuis plusieurs semaines maintenant, les bandes-annonces de L’Amour est dans le pré 2026 teasent l’épisode sur Justine à travers des extraits montrant notamment l’épreuve du speed dating. Ce lundi 14 septembre, le quatrième épisode, déjà disponible sur M6+, arrive donc enfin à la télévision, pour le plus grand bonheur des téléspectateurs. Et le moins que l’on puisse dire est que l’émission réserve bien des surprises, autant aux agriculteurs qu’aux fidèles du programme.

Dans l’épisode 4 de la saison 21 de L’Amour est dans le pré, diffusé ce lundi soir dès 21 h 10 sur M6, Justine doit faire face à de nombreuses complications qui ont forcément impacté son aventure.

Sommaire

L’Amour est dans le pré 2026 : le rendez-vous de Justine et Audran a viré au cauchemar…

Les spectateurs remarqueront que lors de son rendez-vous avec Audran, Justine n’est pas restée très immobile. En effet, à plusieurs reprises, la trentenaire a quitté le bateau pour prendre l’air. La raison ? Justine a le mal de mer. Malgré les précautions prises par la production, l’étape de la péniche était obligatoire pour le speed dating. Ainsi, l’agricultrice a dû faire face à ses peurs, mais cela n’a pas duré longtemps.

Interrogée par Télé Star sur cette expérience, Justine a déclaré qu’elle n’a malheureusement pas réussi à surmonter cette épreuve : « J’avais prévenu la production, mais j’ai pensé qu’en étant sur une péniche, à quai, sur la Seine, ça irait. Mais ça a été chaotique. Ça a tangué dans tous les sens, dans mon corps et dans ma tête. Les émotions étaient décuplées et je n’étais pas moi-même. Je lui ai fait vivre le pire date de toute sa vie« .

Voilà donc qui vient instantanément expliquer son comportement particulier envers Audran. Mais ce n’est pas tout ! Justine a également dû faire face à un désistement de dernière minute, qu’elle a encore du mal à digérer aujourd’hui…

Pourquoi Clément s’est désisté dans L’Amour est dans le pré 2026 ?

Alors que Justine s’apprêtait à annoncer à Audran et Clément qu’ils ont été choisis pour l’accompagner à la ferme, le prétendant de 24 ans et éducateur sportif, décide de prendre la main sur la situation en lui annonçant qu’il ne souhaite plus continuer l’émission à ses côtés. « C’était juste pour te dire que je ne vais pas donner suite malheureusement. Je n’ai pas eu ce petit coup de cœur même si tu es une nana magnifique. Je préfère stopper là et ne pas te donner de faux espoirs« , lui a alors annoncé Clément en face-à-face.

Toujours au micro de Télé Star, Justine n’a pas hésité à revenir sur cette trahison : « Ça m’a vraiment déçue. Pour moi, j’étais l’objet d’un pari avec ses copains, et j’ai trouvé ça dénigrant. » Justine était, en effet, tombée sous le charme de Clément, mais l’attirance n’était donc pas réciproque. À voir maintenant ce que l’avenir lui réserve au sein du jeu.

Suis-nous sur Google pour ne rien rater de nos quiz et actus séries

Drifa Maza

Journaliste

Journaliste chez Serieously depuis 2023, Drifa Maza est une grande passionnée de cinéma de toutes les époques, allant de ses débuts silencieux en noir et blanc à aujourd’hui. Toujours à l’affut de l’actualité, elle ne rate aucune sortie ciné et série, et est toujours à la recherche d’une nouveauté et d’un show à binger. Son enfance a été bercée par les films Pixar et l’ère Disney Channel, son adolescence par le genre de la dystopie et les Marvel (qu’elle aime toujours autant) mais c’est surtout en regardant La La Land en 2016 que son amour pour cette industrie est né. Aujourd’hui, Drifa adore partager cette passion et ses connaissances à travers des articles, des quiz et des interviews et rencontres avec les actrices, acteurs et cinéastes comme Celine Song, Danny Boyle ou encore Tom Hardy et Timothée Chalamet, qu’elle admire.

item.title: [HuffPost] After A Long Marriage, I Started Dating Again In My 50s. I Didn’t Expect The Reaction I Got From Much-Younger Men.
item.dc:creator: Hilary Rubin
item.description: After my divorce settled, and following years spent raising my children and caring for my mother in her final chapter, I began to dip my toe back into the dating pool at 51. item.content:encoded:
After my divorce settled, and following years spent raising my children and caring for my mother in her final chapter, I began to dip my toe back into the dating pool at 51.
Even though I felt ready to open up to the possibility of romance, I was also very aware of my emotional capacity ― what I had the bandwidth to hold and what I didn’t. I wasn’t looking for a soulmate, nor was I interested in future-tripping, making long-term promises or auditioning for a major role in a partner’s established life.
Before my marriage, my natural inclination had always been toward older men ― men with established footholds, refined perspectives and the gravitational pull of maturity. But after a long marriage and years of caregiving, my needs had shifted. I simply did not have the emotional reserve to play a significant role in a partner’s existing domestic ecosystem.
Given that, and at the behest of my curious married friends who urged me to “take one for the team,” I manually adjusted my age preferences on the apps, sliding the scale far enough left that it could be framed as a cultural statement. I widened those parameters not as a hunt but as an experiment in lowering the stakes. I assumed I was simply opening a doorway to casual conversation. What I didn’t expect was the immediate, enthusiastic response from men 10, 15 and 20 years my junior.
Unlike men in my own demographic, who often carried the weight of past domestic entanglements or rigid expectations, these younger suitors approached dating with refreshing candor, often addressing the age gap upfront with curiosity rather than hesitation, viewing it not as an obstacle but as a primary attraction.
I quickly realized this wasn’t an anomaly; I had stumbled onto a quiet, deliberate movement of young men actively seeking out older women.
Of course, it’s impossible to address this cultural wave without confronting the hyper-sexualized “cougar” or “MILF” tropes that are pervasive in the media. As a result, a not-insignificant portion of the messages in my inbox was inevitably fueled purely by a fantasy that reduced an older woman to an erotic milestone rather than a person. Distinguishing genuine intrigue from fetishization was the primary task of navigating this pool.
Still, a substantial segment of these younger men started surprisingly earnest conversations, and one young professional immediately stood out. He was 36 to my 51, but far more mature than his peers, intensely focused on his career, yet looking for adult female companionship.
What began as a series of engaging dinners turned into a meaningful, purposeful connection for both of us. For him, it offered a space to laugh, share and connect, entirely free from the biological clock and domestic pressure cooker of peer-group dating. For me, it served as a gentle, low-stakes step back into a dating landscape I hadn’t navigated in nearly two decades.
Our relationship spanned roughly 18 months ― a fluid, unhurried arrangement anchored in complete transparency, mutual discretion and shared pleasure, deliberately unburdened by demands for formal exclusivity or traditional milestones. We remain friends today, and while he still occasionally gives a quiet wink asking to return to that season, we mostly laugh about our time together.
Recently, on a getaway to an upscale Southern California suburb, I overheard a hotel concierge advising guests on a few local restaurants — playfully referred to as “cougar bars” — where younger men gather specifically in hopes of meeting women their senior. Who would have thought? What I quietly discovered on the fringes of dating app filters had spilled into everyday public life.
For generations, the older-man-younger-woman dynamic wasn’t just tolerated; it was the default social blueprint. When high-profile men married partners decades their junior, culture treated it as a standard perk of status and wealth. Society rarely questioned their motives or demanded they defend their choices.
Meanwhile, when the gender roles were reversed, we coined the term “cougar” to paint older women as predatory or desperate, and the younger men who dated them as novelties or “boy toys.” High-profile exceptions, like Demi Moore and Ashton Kutcher, were usually treated as tabloid anomalies or public spectacles.
Today, that archaic framework is fracturing, largely driven by the cold mechanics of modern dating technology. According to Pew Research, 63% of men under 30 report being single, compared to just 34% of women in the same age bracket. Furthermore, 64% of men report feeling insecure due to a staggering lack of incoming messages on apps. On platforms like Tinder, where the average match rate for men sits at a dismal 5%, young men face a brutal numbers game.
To survive the feed, younger men have learned to game the system. On Bumble and Hinge, a 26-year-old man has to manually slide his age preferences upward to appear in a 50-something or 60-something woman’s queue. Widening his age bracket may partly be a numerical calculation to expand his reach, but it is also a deliberate tactical shift. Rather than chasing low response rates among his peers, he may recognize that mature women operate with far greater clarity, efficiency and directness, making an interaction not only more statistically probable but also of higher baseline quality.
Bumble’s global data shows that nearly 60% of women are open to dating younger men. Meanwhile, Hinge Labs reports that 65% of young men want deep emotional intimacy early on, yet nearly half hold back, perhaps for fear of failing to meet the intense life-stage expectations of women their own age.
This brings us to the core of the dynamic. As The New York Times recently highlighted in its exploration of why younger men are seeking out mature women, featuring commentary from writer Emily Leibert and psychoanalyst Jamieson Webster, this phenomenon sits at the intersection of female liberation and male risk-aversion.
A mature, established woman may act as an oasis for a younger man, offering high-value connection, emotional composure and engaging conversation without demanding that he immediately step into the role of provider, husband or father.
In a culture where young men are overwhelmed by economic instability and shifting relationship expectations, seeking out an older woman may function as a shortcut to low-pressure connection. If she has her own financial stability, her own home and her own identity, she probably isn’t asking him to build a life with her. Her life is already built.
Yet that’s where the friction lies.
Some younger men are drawn to an older woman under the naive assumption that her self-sufficiency will make her “low maintenance.” Younger men may mistake an established woman’s independence for a lack of standards, assuming that because she doesn’t need his financial support or a traditional commitment, she requires minimal effort.
The reality, of course, is the exact opposite. True self-sufficiency comes with firm boundaries, high standards and zero tolerance for playing a supporting role in someone else’s unwritten script. An older woman who has raised children, built a career or cared for aging parents knows the exact value of her time and emotional investment.
Today, at 62, I look back on that chapter of my life with gratitude, but also with clarity. As a single woman now, my desires have shifted once again, and so has my capacity.
While I still open dating apps occasionally, mostly while traveling, my criteria have evolved. I’ve reopened my bracket to men in their early 50s and beyond, seeking the sharp, intellectually vibrant partners I’ve always aligned with best. I am no longer seeking the low-bandwidth, transitional space that post-divorce life required. Now I’m looking for someone ready for 30-plus years of shared curiosity and real depth.
While Kinsey Institute survey data shows that older women report higher levels of relationship satisfaction and commitment when dating younger men, I believe that satisfaction relies entirely on mutual transparency.
Hilary Rubin is an essayist and model examining performance, physical autonomy, and modern cultural dynamics. You can follow her work on Instagram @hilaryrubin or at hilaryrubin.com.

item.content:encoded:
The Ralph Lauren womenswear brand is a love letter to the designer’s wife of more than 60 years.
Ricky Lauren, his lifelong muse, is present in each of the designer’s collections.
At the designer’s New York Fashion Week show, Ricky Lauren sat front row along with other members of the Lauren family as her husband took guests on a whirlwind romantic escape ahead of the official launch of New York Fashion Week.
Actors Meghann Fahy, Cynthia Erivo, Viola Davis, Elizabeth Debicki and Ella Hunt were a few of the celebrity guests in attendance at the downtown Manhattan show.
“Ralph just generally designs so beautifully for a woman’s body,” Hunt told The Associated Press after the show.
Lauren pared down the lavish setting from his fall ready-to-wear show of opulent rugs and antique chairs, keeping the setting white and minimalist with attendees sitting on ivory fabric benches and models emerging from behind white doors.
Models glided down the rows of fashionable guests in soft and sensual silhouettes with a color palette of navy and white to the tunes of love songs, including “Every Little Thing She Does Is Magic” by The Police.
For Lauren, the collection was an “irreverent take on romance” that “upends traditional notions of chic.”
“It’s about ways of dressing that celebrate ingenuity, character, and originality — the freedom and fun of creating a style that is truly personal,” the designer said in his show notes.
Lauren opened the show with a white corseted top and white tailored pants before an array of deep, rich blues unfurled down the runway.
The 86-year-old designer played with his signature tailored designs incorporating billowing white pinstriped pants and dramatic floor-length overcoats.
Lauren accentuated his refined looks with touches of flair from oversized flowered brooches, feathered bolero jackets draped over evening gowns with plunging necklines to fringed scarves tied at the waist. While some models strutted in heels, others walked the runway in slipper-like flats. Either way, the models looked ready to jet off on a European getaway in their elegantly laid-back white pants and straw hats or pose on a red carpet in his evening gowns.
“What Ralph Lauren is doing this year is writing through his clothes about a very kind of modern dream,” David Lauren, the label’s chief branding and innovation officer, said.
In his classic take of mixing the masculine and feminine, Lauren overlaid a golden fringed gown over a pair of navy trousers, and in an homage to his first suit for women, the designer featured two pantsuits in his collection.
Lauren even brought out a youthful side to his modern romance story, pairing slim-fitting jackets with low-slung pants and distressed denim.
“What I love about coming to a Ralph Lauren show and wearing Ralph Lauren is that no matter where I am in time or space, or as I’m growing and changing in my styles and preferences and tastes change, I can grow with Ralph,” Ariana DeBose said.
The stylish crowd was eager to catch a glimpse of Lauren as the line of models returned behind the doors to close the show. As the applause rang out, Lauren arrived in his aviator glasses and varsity jacket to wave to his guests before his wife, Ricky, joined him with a kiss.
Associated Press journalist Brooke Lefferts contributed to this report.
